Makris demonstrated that once one robot is compromised, all Yarbo robots worldwide can be accessed, giving a hacker control over thousands of mowers. He also found that Yarbo's telemetry is routed to ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, and that despite being listed as headquartered in New York, Yarbo appears to operate out of Shenzhen, China. When Makris contacted Yarbo about the vulnerability, the company downplayed the issue, claiming the security flaw was a deliberate design decision intended to 'provide timely and accurate solutions to mechanical or software concerns.' Makris then disclosed the findings to The Verge, which confirmed and publicized the vulnerability. Reported impact With control of a Yarbo robot, an attacker can remotely operate the 200-pound mower and override its safety features, including disabling emergency stop buttons. Makris demonstrated this by remotely controlling a Yarbo mower over a 6,000-mile distance. Hackers could access customer data including GPS coordinates, emails, Wi-Fi passwords, and video footage from the robots' built-in cameras. The robots could also be enlisted into a botnet to conduct illegal activity through an owner's network. Index analysis The vulnerability affects approximately 11,000 Yarbo robot lawn mowers worldwide. The security flaw stems from the use of a universal, unchangeable root password and the lack of any user override or permanent password change capability. Governance controls Yarbo characterized the security vulnerability as an intentional design decision rather than acknowledging it as a security flaw requiring remediation.
AII-1000-77377: Between May 1 and 3, 2026, Ghana Police Service's Cyber Vetting and Enforcement Team (CVET) conducted coordinated cyber operations across Sogakope, Dabala, Tongu, Akatsi and Aflao in the Volta Region, arresting five suspects: Raphael Ablordeppey (32), Anipah Jonathan (23), Dzamesi Bright Kofi (35), Thomas Ayoyo (17) and Louis Segbawu (18) following intelligence on a group creating and circulating AI-generated videos impersonating President John Dramani Mahama. On May 4, 2026, further cyber field tracking operations led to the arrest of six additional suspects in Aflao: five Nigerians—Bishop Esiri (46), Wisdom James (25), Ali Lucky (23), Edwin Edos (22), and John Kofi Darlington (20)—and one Ghanaian, Danu Peter (19). Police retrieved laptop computers, mobile phones, internet routers, 120 pre-registered SIM cards, and a Nigerian-registered vehicle. Reported impact According to police, preliminary investigations indicate that the suspects used fraudulent AI-generated content to solicit money and sensitive personal information from unsuspecting members of the public through online platforms. The suspects are part of a wider network engaged in the creation and dissemination of fraudulent digital contents designed to impersonate high-profile personalities for financial gains. Index analysis A deepfake is a hyper-realistic video or audio clip generated by artificial intelligence in which a person's face, voice, or both are digitally manipulated to make them appear to say or do things they never did. AI tools that can generate convincing deepfake videos are now widely available online, often for free, making the technology dangerously accessible. Governance controls In court on May 6, 2026, nine of the 11 suspects were remanded into police custody to reappear on May 25, 2026, while Thomas Ayoyo and Louis Segbawu were granted bail with two sureties each to be justified.
AII-1000-77337: Stripe CEO Patrick Collison reported that token theft now affects one in every six new sign-ups at AI companies using the payment platform. Fraudsters create fake accounts to steal tokens used to buy computing power, either reselling them or using them for unauthorized purposes. Token fraud has doubled over the past six months, with attackers using automated agents to consume tokens in minutes. Traditional fraud teams cannot react fast enough to prevent the attacks. Reported impact AI startups face massive computing bills they never authorized, as attackers burn inference costs at machine speed. Some companies have discontinued free trial offerings due to the cost of token theft. For eight high-growth AI businesses using Stripe's updated Radar fraud detection tool, more than 3.3 million risky sign-ups were blocked in a single recent month. Index analysis The attack vector exploits the economics of AI services, where sign-ups include valuable compute tokens that differ from traditional software trials. Fraudsters leverage automated agents to consume these tokens faster than human fraud teams can respond. Governance controls Stripe expanded its Radar fraud detection system to scan sign-ups and usage in real time, assigning risk scores based on IP addresses, email domains, and device fingerprints. ElevenLabs and Lovable have deployed the updated tool.
AII-1000-77323: Baidu's AI Smart Answer feature generated false information describing Nanjing lawyer Li Xiaoliang as having received a three-year prison sentence, displayed alongside his photograph in search results. Li Xiaoliang discovered the false content in 2024 on Baidu's mobile app and website. A media company discovered that searching for television drama titles on an AI search platform returned pirated streaming links positioned at the top of results, with text such as 'no extraction code needed.' Reported impact Li Xiaoliang's social reputation was damaged by the false defamatory content generated by Baidu's AI system, affecting his professional and personal life. The pirated links in the AI search results infringed the media company's information network distribution rights for the copyrighted television dramas. Index analysis Nanjing Jiangbei Xinqu Court found that while Baidu's regular search suggestions and related searches derived from user search records without direct processing, the 'AI Smart Answer' feature involved AI technology processing and generation of content explicitly indicating negative information about Li Xiaoliang. The court determined Baidu was negligent despite claiming AI hallucinations are unpredictable and accidental. Shanghai Xuhui District Court found that the AI search platform, based on large language models and retrieval-augmented generation technology, cannot avoid indexing and displaying content from public internet sources. The court determined the platform did not manually edit or recommend results and had no subjective fault, and that it had fulfilled its obligations by maintaining complaint channels and promptly removing infringing content upon notification. Governance controls Baidu appealed its first-instance judgment on grounds that AI systems cannot predict user queries or fully avoid hallucinations, but the Nanjing Intermediate Court rejected this argument, noting that other AI platforms such as Douyin and DeepSeek did not produce similar defamatory results. The AI search platform demonstrated due diligence through model and algorithm registration, establishing complaint channels, and removing infringing links on the same day a lawyer's notice was received.
